name: Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate
lead: Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB), sold as Uvinul A Plus (BASF) and Parsol DHHB (DSM), is an oil-soluble organic UVA filter with an absorption maximum near 354 nm, noted for photostability and compatibility with other UV absorbers.[1][2]

The EU approved it for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10%, and it is also approved in several other markets including Japan; in the US, Wikipedia says it may be used for product protection rather than as a sunscreen active.[1]

Published work on DHHB specifically is mostly laboratory-based: filter-filter photochemistry, formulation, and beach environmental monitoring. A notable regulatory discussion concerns a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate. No clinical trial of DHHB alone was found.

paras: DHHB is made by reacting 3-hydroxy-N,N-diethylaniline with phthalic anhydride and esterifying the product with 1-hexanol.[1] It is used in sunscreens and SPF cosmetics, often with UVB filters, and studies of filter-filter interactions examine how filters photostabilise one another and quench excited states.[3] Formulation research has tested it in nanostructured lipid carriers and nanoemulsions for photostability and skin penetration,[4] and in sprayable emulsions.[5]
A US drug label lists it, alongside ethylhexyl triazone, bisoctrizole and diethylhexyl butamido triazone, in a sunscreen product.[6]

Wikipedia describes DHHB as a safe sunscreen ingredient, with the main concern being the contaminant di-n-hexyl phthalate, which the European Chemicals Agency listed as a Substance of Very High Concern in 2013.[1] The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety recommended a maximum of 260 ppm of this contaminant, with a target below 1 ppm because the contamination is avoidable.[1] Grokipedia cites the SCCS as confirming safety up to 10% with impurities controlled, and reports minimal percutaneous absorption in animal models.[2]

Eight UV filters, a group that included DHHB, were measured on Gran Canaria beaches in a 2015 environmental risk assessment,[7] and DHHB was among ten filters tested on brine shrimp and marine microalgae.[8]
No studies found. Related laboratory research is limited to the photochemistry, formulation and environmental studies cited above.

card.summary: A photostable UVA sunscreen filter common outside the US; evidence is lab-based and regulatory.
card.aka: DHHB, Uvinul A Plus, Parsol DHHB
card.note: Not a US sunscreen active; EU advisers set limits on a phthalate contaminant.

quick.overview:
DHHB is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVA light. It is photostable and used in products in the EU, Japan and other markets.

It is not a US-approved sunscreen active, and no clinical trials of it alone were found.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVA near 354 nm and dissipates the energy, and studies show it interacts with other filters to help stabilise them.
quick.risks: The main regulatory concern is a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate, for which EU advisers recommended strict limits. Environmental monitoring studies have detected UV filters on beaches.
